❌ Rejected the contribution.
Comment: This problem is too difficult for a clash. Consider making this a puzzle instead :)

✅ Approved the contribution.
Comment: Great problem for a clash. Can be solved either with dynamic programming or just with really dumb bruteforce.

This is a very cool idea, but i think it's a little too difficult for a short clash. On top of that, I'm pretty sure test 4 can be done with seven "1"s (1111 - 111 = 1000). I think validator 4 as well, can be done shorter (1111 - 111 - 1 = 999).
This is quite a big task for a clash and might be too difficult for most players to even start the problem. Consider making this a puzzle instead :)

Cases
* Validator 2: Please change [[n]] to a 1-digit integer to match Test 2.

* Test 3: Please change [[n]] to a 3-digit integer to match Validator 3.

Thanks.
Maybe a lot. Is 11 in the decimal system?

Please swap Pair 4 and Pair 5. In general, cases should be ordered by increasing complexity or magnitude of inputs and outputs (except that the first pair also serves as an illustrative example, so putting the case of n = 1 there isn't a good idea.)

Thanks.
It can be solved by bruteforce. It's a bit too easy for a puzzle.
Subtraction isn't an allowed operation for this clash.
Ah I didn't notice! Thanks for telling me.
What do you mean by brute force? Selecting '1', '+', 'x', '(', or ')' at each position? Even this method is too difficult (in my opinion) for most players to implement.

This is still a DP-like approach involving memoization to cut down compute on previously-seen values.

Your solution, much like the author's solution, doesn't inherently explain how one should think about this problem. The involvement of parenthesised equations here is part of the trick - understanding that you can substitute any value into the final equation as long as you have determined the equation to obtain said value is a crucial step in identifying this problem as recursive overlapping subproblems.

In general, DP is, in my opinion, not suitable for a clash. I've had clashes rejected before for "simpler", more "brute force" intended solutions; eg involving BFS to explore the entire search space. This clash takes that one step further as the search space here is (likely) too large to completely explore.

So to summarise, there are a few key points that make this clash "too hard":
- tricky simplification
- large and hard-to-define search space
- requires breaking down into smaller subproblems (DP)

Hope this explains my thought process more clearly :)
Also, if this is too easy to be a puzzle, the problem can be made harder with some small tweaks (e.g., allowing the subtraction operation).

The search space is not too large to explore, at all.

There are only 1000 possible values. The whole point of not allowing subtraction and division is that a+b is always greater than a and greater than b, and a*b is always greater than a and greater than b, so the only values you ever need to consider are the thousand numbers 1 to 1000.

That's why the bruteforce solution is so easy.

I don't understand what you mean by "doesn't explain how to think about this problem".

If you can build a in s steps and b in t steps then you can build a+b and a*b in s+t steps. That's all there is to understand about the problem. You can call it dynamic programming or Dijkstra or breadth-first-search if you like fancy concepts, but really it's just a really dumb bruteforce that keeps adding the s+t steps to a+b and a*b when you have s steps for a and t steps for b.
